transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The Trump administration appears to be expanding its campaign of taxpayer-funded TV ads promoting
President Trump.
The White House describes these as public service announcements, but lawmakers from
both parties have criticized them as propaganda.
The White House defends the ads as educational and patriotic.
The number of U.S. troops who have died or been wounded in the Iran war continues to
rise.
Medicare's Quill Lawrence reports 19 service members have died and 861 wounded.
18 U.S. troops have died in combat since the war began in February, and this week the Army
announced an additional officer died, not in combat, after she fell ill on a flight
toward the region.
The number of wounded in action has also crept up, including a number of traumatic brain
injuries that can take weeks to diagnose.
The Pentagon has said that most of the wounded have been able to return to duty.
The strain of long deployments is also taking a toll. While President Trump initially and
repeatedly said the war would be over in days or weeks, it has included a record-breaking
nine months at sea for the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Group, which is now en route home.
The Navy confirmed this week that at least eight sailors attempted suicide during that
tour.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
The Supreme Court is allowing states to resume using a controversial federal tool to check
voter eligibility before the November elections. A lower court had blocked the use of the systematic
alien verification for entitlements, or SAVE, program, saying it violates voter privacy
and can lead to wrongful voter purges.
Voting law experts say that a rule barring systematic voter purges 90 days before an
election will likely limit the ruling's impact on the midterms.
New polls out this week paint a mixed picture of how people feel about A.I., and Piers Windsor
Johnston reports the surveys come amid calls from industry leaders to slow development
of the rapidly changing technology.
A new Reuters/Epsos poll found 73 percent of Americans worry that A.I. companies are
not doing enough to prevent serious harm. Harvard Medical School psychologist Luanna
Marquez says those concerns make sense, but people need a way to stay informed about the
risks of A.I. without getting overwhelmed by every warning.
I think you're looking at data in a balanced way, trying to take your emotions out, and
not drinking out of a fire hose. I think if you're every day and go, "What's happening
to A.I. today?" You're basically activating that threat in your brain.
In a separate Gallup poll, 34 out of 37 countries surveyed said they feel optimistic about A.I.,
but three out of four Americans told Gallup A.I. worries them.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
Currents on Hawaii's Big Island are bracing for potentially life-threatening and catastrophic
flooding from Hurricane NOLO. The U.S. National Weather Service says tropical storm conditions
are expected to begin on land in the evening. Meanwhile, Mexico is still under threat of
another Pacific hurricane, Polo.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Volkswagen says it's recalling 2.86 million Volkswagen and Audi-branded vehicles as a
precautionary measure over a screw whose failure could cause a loss of steering. The affected
vehicles are Volkswagen Tiguan, Touran, Golf Golf, variant and Caddy models built between
2013 and 2024, and Audi Q3 models made between 2017 and 2024.
A federal judge in Oklahoma handed a win to a Jewish charter school this week. State Impact
Oklahoma's Beth Wallace reports this would be the nation's first publicly-funded religious
school.
This year, a state board rejected the application for Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School, a virtual
school providing religious education. The board relied on a 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court
ruling for a similar case with a Catholic school. Now, a judge says that rejection was
discriminatory. Rachel Lazzer is the president of Americans United for Separation of Church
and State, which has joined the case.
We're directly funding with taxpayer money, religious education, and turning government
schools into religious government schools.
If appealed, the case could wind up before the U.S. Supreme Court, which was split on
a similar case last year. For NPR News, I'm Beth Wallace in Tulsa.
The robotic spacecraft that failed to rescue an aging NASA telescope has plunged back to
Earth less than three months after launching. It reentered the atmosphere overnight, bringing
the $30 million salvage effort of NASA's Swift Observatory to a close.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Trump administration expands campaign of taxpayer-funded TV ads promoting President Trump
19 U.S. service members have died and 861 wounded in Iran war since February
Supreme Court allows states to resume using SAVE program to check voter eligibility
Polls show 73 percent of Americans worry AI companies not doing enough to prevent harm
Hawaii's Big Island braces for potentially catastrophic flooding from Hurricane NOLO
Volkswagen recalls 2.86 million vehicles over screw failure that could cause steering loss
Federal judge rules Oklahoma's rejection of Jewish charter school was discriminatory
Robotic spacecraft fails to rescue aging NASA Swift Observatory, reenters Earth's atmosphere
